chapters.summary: Chair Stevens introduces the oversight hearing on the runaway and homeless youth shelter system, describing DYCD's crisis shelters, transitional independent living programs, street outreach teams, and 24/7 drop-in centers across the five boroughs.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens overview of RHY shelter system and services

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So now, welcome to today's hearing on Children and Youth Committee.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I am Althea Stevens, the chair of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us today's hearing, where this committee will conduct an oversight on the city's runaway and homeless youth shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The city's Department of Youth and Community Development contracts with a range of crisis service shelters, transition independent living shelters, street outreach team, 24-7 drop-in centers across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Today, those programs provide a range of critical services to runaway and homeless youth.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Street outreach teams canvass the city to identify youth and young adults experiencing homelessness, while drop-in centers provide young people with a place to access food, clothing, housing, health care, and transportation, as well as

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: assistance from housing and employment navigations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Crisis centers then provide temporary shelters for youth for up to 120 days.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: While transitional independent living programs provide long-term housing for up to 24 months for young people towards stability and gain independent living services and build economic self-sufficiency,

chapters.summary: Stevens highlights that 319 young people were turned away from shelter between January and June, raises concerns about underfunding, capacity gaps, and the need for mental health, employment, and housing navigation support beyond just beds and meals.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on capacity crisis, 319 youth turned away

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: those services provide a critical lifeline for young people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Despite this important work, serious questions remain about whether the city provides them with the resources.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: resources, capacity necessary to meet the needs of young people in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Today, we hope to learn about the agency's plan to issue a new concept paper and how it would address the evolving needs and costs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm going to say that again.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The cost for facing and delivering those critical services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Beyond funding, we're also deeply concerned about shelter capacity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Between January and June of this year, 319 young people sought shelter were turned away.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No young person who takes the difficult steps of seeking shelter should be left without a place to stay because our shelter system lacks capacity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When RHY system is underfunded or lack capacity, young people fall through dangerous gaps, are left unable to access appropriate services, and gets discharged back into homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Young people experiencing homelessness come into RHY system after experiencing trauma and instability that cannot be addressed by simply providing a bed and a meal.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It is our responsibility as a city to prioritize their mental health and physical health and ensure that housing, employment, and financial navigations are

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: guided them through complex systems and provide the support young people need to achieve long-term stability.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Access.

chapters.summary: Sandra Escamilla-Davies of DYCD shares a personal story about finding her uncle living on the streets with HIV and crack addiction, which shaped her commitment to social work and building ecosystems that prevent disconnection and create pathways back for young people.
chapters.title: Escamilla-Davies shares personal story motivating her RHY work

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Stevens and members of the Committee on Children and Youth.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: My name is Sandra Escamilla-Davies of the New York City Department of Youth and Community Development, and I am joined here today by Executive Deputy Commissioner Susan Haskell, Assistant Commissioner

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Samantha Dawkins, and Tracy Thorne, Senior Director of Runaway Homeless Youth Programs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We are pleased to discuss the effectiveness of the city's runaway homeless youth shelter system today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair Stevens, for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: This issue is deeply personal to me.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: More than 35 years ago, I found a beloved uncle who was a young adult himself at the time, living on the streets, HIV positive, and struggling with crack addiction.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I grew up in a close home and family, and until then, I did not fully understand how a series of events could disconnect someone from the very family, community, and systems of support that might

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Otherwise, hold them up.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That experience was transformational for me.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: It shaped my decision to enter social work and my belief that our responsibility is not simply to respond once someone is in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We have to build an ecosystem around children, young people, and families that helps prevent those disconnection,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: creates pathways back when they occur, and provides the relationship, resources, and opportunities people need not only to stabilize, but to succeed and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Being free from crisis is essential, but it is not the same as being fully prepared for what comes next.

chapters.summary: Escamilla-Davies details DYCD's residential services: 913 total beds serving ages 16-24, including 160 beds for homeless young adults 21-24, with 100 new beds added through council partnership (70 currently serving, 20 opening soon, 10 still being sited).
chapters.title: DYCD overview of RHY residential services and bed capacity

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That belief is at the heart of our Runaway and Homeless Youth programs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Through residential services, drop-in centers, and street outreach, DYCD and our...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Extraordinary provider partners reach more than 40,000 young people annually with services designed to promote stability, connection, independence, and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Our residential services include crisis services program, transitional independent living support programs,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: and across the city, residential programs serve young people ages 16 through 24, providing a total of 913 beds.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: For homeless young adults ages 21 to 24, DYCD funds six programs with a total of 160 beds.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We are grateful that in partnership with the council and under the leadership of Chair Stevens, this capacity was expanded by 100 beds for homeless young adults, strengthening our ability to

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: respond to growing needs of this community.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Of these 100 new beds, 70 are currently serving young people, 20 are scheduled to open shortly, and we continue to work with providers to identify a site for the remaining 10 beds.

chapters.summary: Escamilla-Davies describes DYCD's eight drop-in centers offering food, clothing, counseling, and health workshops with at least one 24/7 center per borough, plus street outreach teams that meet young people where they congregate to provide immediate support and connections to housing.
chapters.title: DYCD on drop-in centers and street outreach programs

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: DYCD also funds eight contract drop-in centers, which, by the way, was my first job, where LGBTQI plus youth and other young people can access essential resources

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: such as food, clothing, and hygiene supplies along counseling, educational, and health workshops, recreational program, and referrals to additional services and shelters when needed.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Specialized staff, including housing navigators, financial coaches, peer navigators, and mental health clinicians work closely with young people to identify their goals and take meaningful steps towards long-term stability and independence.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: To ensure accessibility, at least one drop-in center in every borough operates 24 hours a day and seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Our street outreach programs meet young people where they are, including in locations where runaway and homeless youth are known to congregate.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Outreach teams provide immediate support, information, safety planning, and connections to housing and other critical services.

chapters.summary: Escamilla-Davies explains individualized case management, mental health services, and LGBTQ+ affirming environments across RHY programs, noting the Ali Fournay Center's expertise in serving LGBTQ+ youth who are disproportionately represented among homeless youth.
chapters.title: DYCD on individualized services and LGBTQ+ youth support

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Across the RHY system, providers work with each young person to understand their strength, their needs, and goals.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And from intake and assessment through ongoing case management, young people receive individualized counseling.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: referrals and connections to services that support their overall well-being, including specialized mental health care when appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: All RHY providers are trained to create welcoming and affirming environments for LGBTQI+,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: young people who are disproportionately represented among young people experiencing homelessness and may face family rejection and additional barriers to housing and employment.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Our system also includes mission-driven organizations such as the Aliforni Center with particular expertise in serving LGBTQI plus young people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: This work includes professional development related to sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression, gender-affirming interactions, physically safe and culturally responsive environments, and swift response to bias and discrimination.

chapters.summary: Escamilla-Davies describes how counselors develop individualized service plans with short and long-term goals, connecting youth to health services, education, career development, substance use prevention, and family reunification, with the ultimate goal of leaving youth more connected than when they entered the system.
chapters.title: DYCD on service plans, counseling, and program goals

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And RHY programs, I just got to say, I mean, the work that providers do is intense, intentional, and incredible.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: In RHY programs, counselors work collaboratively with young people to develop individualized service plans that establish both short-term and long-term goals.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Through direct service and community partnerships, young people can access physical and mental health services, educational and career development opportunities, substance use prevention services, violence

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: interventions and prevention counseling, financial coaching and housing assistance.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: When appropriate,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Providers also support family reunification to help young people transition to longer-term housing and supportive programs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Ultimately, our goal is not simply to help a young person move through a moment of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: As I said before, it is to help them ensure that they leave our system more connected than when they entered, connected to stable housing, to caring adults, to education and employment, to health and mental health support, and a community that continue to support them.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: This is how we help young people move from stability towards opportunity and ultimately to...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Towards thriving.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to discuss DYCD's Runaway Homeless Youth Programming.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We remain committed to working alongside the council, providers, advocates, and most importantly, young people with lived experiences, strengthening the system and to expand opportunity for young people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We are pleased to answer any questions you may have.

chapters.summary: Stevens presses DYCD on why no new RFP has been issued since 2018, with the system operating under contract extensions through June 2027. Escamilla-Davies acknowledges the 2018 RFP gap and says she is working with OMB and the deputy mayor on stabilization before procurement.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens questions DYCD on RFP delays since 2018

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I will jump right into my questions because we have a lot.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm going to start off just talking about the RFP and contracting process because this has been a longstanding issue.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: DYCD has not issued a new RFP for...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: For RHY drop-in centers, outreach, crisis, shelters, TIL programs since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Instead, the agencies have relied on contract amendments and negotiation acquisitions and extensions to continue those services through June.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As a result, the RHY system continues to operate under contracts stemming from procurement issues approximately nine years ago.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What does DYCD plan to issue a new concept paper RFP for RHY services?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I can say that since I started in this position in February, and as a former provider who has done direct service for over 30 years, I have been committed to really thinking about the ways in which we

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: pay providers on time and adequately.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So the 2018 last RFP is really felt, and we have that same issue with other contracts as well.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Our HY in particular is a priority to me because it is one of the, I guess,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: the one that is the longest in procurement.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And yet what I know needs to happen, because from concept paper to implementation, it could take anywhere from two years.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And so I am in the process of speaking to the deputy mayor and working with OMB to really think about how we begin to create some stabilization, including by considering ways in which to bring the rate

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: and the resources at a certain level before procurement.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about a 2022 $15 million federal grant and a concept paper that would have increased provider reimbursement rates but was tabled by OMB. Susan Haskell clarifies the grant was HUD's Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program funding street outreach, rapid rehousing, and permanent housing services, not a concept paper for an RFP.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on $15M federal grant and concept paper status

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In 2022, New York City was promised a $15 million federal grant as part of its commitment to prevent and end homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In connection with this initiative, DYCD issued a concept paper and developed an RFP that would have increased providers' per-bred reimbursement rates.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: However, the RFP was substantially tabled by OMB.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What is the status of that RFP, and does DYCD plan to release it?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Hi, Susan.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: In 2022 was actually a really exciting time for Runaway and Homeless Youth Services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We pulled together a broad swath of stakeholders to discuss what was needed to end youth homelessness, and it gave us an opportunity to try some new services, including...

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Peer navigation, housing navigation, financial literacy, that yielded a report, an accountability report, really, with recommendations that DYCD

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: when operationalized to, with our partnerships, with ACS, with DSS, with our other partners to meet those goals.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And that's been an ongoing process since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a concept paper, and it wasn't planned to be a request for a proposal.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: It was a stakeholder engagement and planning that yielded a report, which was the mayor's report to end youth homelessness in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And we continue to reflect on those recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We've implemented so many of them and stay in touch with the committee.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So that's...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That $15 million, that was the grant from the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That was all used just to create this report.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: No, I'm going to turn to my colleague to speak more about the $15 million, but that was a grant from HUD that went, in some cases, directly to providers, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Some of it came to DYCD for the planning, but largely the investment that DYCD made in response to that was CTL funding.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Most of the HUD funding was directly to providers or as part of the planning process.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So most of it was, so none of it was to, it was for the report and it went to some different fundings for some of the programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So that's where all the money was allocated for?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Yeah, I can add a little bit more context.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: There were...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you speak into the mic and play?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Oh, it's not.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's on, but I know I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: The grant was the Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: It's a multi-year grant.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And there were three types of programs that were funded through that grant.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Street outreach.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Rapid rehousing programs and services to support young people to access permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And that work has been folded into the New York City Continuum of Care work through HUD and is in continuous.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: refunded.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: So we funded several providers for those three programs.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: The rapid rehousing had multiple contracts, and that's where the bulk of the money was.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: And those programs were RFPed out and responded to.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: And that's probably the concept paper that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: And now it's part...

utterances.speaker: Samantha Dawkins
utterances.text: Back with the COC and the funding continues and the work continues.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, because when I spoke to providers, they said that this concept paper had came out in the RFP, but they didn't know where it was.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I would like to acknowledge Councilman Rose, who has joined us.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks what steps DYCD is taking to ensure the RFP is released before current extensions expire. Escamilla-Davies explains DYCD is conducting needs assessments, utilization analysis, and cost evaluations across all programs, proposing a larger strategy RFP rather than single-program procurements.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on steps to release RFP before contract extension expires

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What are the steps the agency is taking to ensure the RFP is released and contracts are awarded before the current extension expires?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So we currently, and I think in my broader hearing at the beginning of the year, we currently were doing an analysis of all of our contracts, specifically thinking about them in relationship to utilization and need in the field.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So right now we are trying to determine across New York City what does each community need and whether our programs are being responsive to that need.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Because I'll give you a perfect example, is that we had a provider who was awarded a contract and gave it back to us, not in RHI, but for another procurement.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And they said,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: This is not the need of our neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We need actually services for our older youth.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And so we are going to be doing a needs assessment and a utilization threshold, as well as doing an analysis of what the current...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: cost of doing work is.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And when I say current costs, I mean the current costs at the point of service for the provider, right?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Especially with RHI, that is really important, given the complexity that is needed to address the myriad of needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We're also doing a cost analysis of what it takes for DYCD to run this program effectively.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think you've heard me say, Chair Stevens, that we have grown from a $250 million organization to a $1.6 billion organization in the last 10 years without the same pace in terms of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And so we are deep in that analysis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And then based on that, we are really proposing a strategy, an RFP that in the interim, we're trying to raise the base of some of our contracts, again, in consultation and in coordination with OMB and the mayor's office.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We're going to see where we land.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: But also a path forward is also to figure out, are there things that we could do in the immediate steps to do that?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And then in the long term, is there an RFP that is about a larger strategy as opposed to one intervention or one program?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks for a timeline on DYCD's evaluation and whether a continuous assessment policy will be implemented. Escamilla-Davies says financial analysis is underway, with program-specific analysis in 2-3 months and utilization/needs assessment within a year, activating the Interagency Coordinating Council to align outcomes across agencies.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on evaluation timeline and continuous assessment policy

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So even in some of the stuff you're speaking about, what's the timeline for this evaluation?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And then also just thinking about, are you going to implement something or a policy that will allow for that to be continuous?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because that's one of the things that I've been banging my head about for the last three years about how do we make sure that we're continuing to continue.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: continuously evaluating, ensuring that these programs are meeting the needs, making sure we're including young people and parents and families and part of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that should be something that's continuous so that we're not waiting for an RFP or like now we're in a place where we have an extended contract that

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: you're in the process of doing an evaluation, also doing a cost analysis and all these things at one time,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: is there going to be a policy that you're thinking about implementing that would have continuous evaluation so that when you get to this place that you are not coming in trying to do all these different things?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate the question.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: In terms of a timeline, we are trying to get, we have done a financial analysis of the costs of DYCD.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So that is kind of, we're in the first phase and we are in the process of doing that for each of our programs in the next two to three months.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And then I would say in the next year is like a utilization.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Assessment as well as a needs assessment.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: It will take us within the next year to do that effectively and we're hoping to do it in partnership with sister agencies because at the end of the day these needs will are reflective of all of our work and we are activating our ICC which tell me what the acronym stands for again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Interagency Coordinating Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Don't get me started with the interagency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's everybody who works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are talking.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Yeah, everybody who works directly with young people.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So the commissioners, we're activating that.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: DM Artiaga and I have talked about really coming up with clear outcomes that we want for young people and then how we galvanize our respective.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: portfolios, including our resources on how to meet that need.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So, and how to assess the need across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And so I appreciate the question around assessment.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think that part of what we've done, we have ongoing assessments for all of our programs, but we are looking towards an eye of stabilization and we're looking towards an eye of thinking about expansion in a different way or a new strategy.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So I would say we are now taking what is methodical yearly evaluations with a different lens.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And I appreciate the question about policy, and I'd love to talk to my team about how we make this part of the fabric.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's just so important that we're looking at this and not always just in crisis mode.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And it's so important for us to not only just say that we have the programs, but also assessing the impact and also having a mechanism where

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: participants and providers and families can have a say in it and thinking about how this can be more interactive.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because they're ultimately the ones that should be shaping these programs and, you know, telling us what their needs are.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Can I add one more thing that I think is, as we're assessing needs, we're also looking at, like, what we want to be held accountable in relationship to children, youth, and families.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So, like, are there things that we want to assess in terms of social determinants of health, right, and how we move the needle on those things, especially if we're looking at interagency investments?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That is going to take a while because right now, as an agency, we are contracting and we're monitoring, right, like attendance, participations, you know,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Kids in beds and we want to move to impact and we want to move also to indicators that are not just about prevention but also about resiliency.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah agreed these are things clearly you were listening to my hearings from three years ago and she was like I'm gonna come in and say the things that councilman receives has been yelling about so appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And just know that we're on the same page, just because everybody knows she's a provider.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And this is how providers speak.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So, you know, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens questions whether current per-bed rates of $47,000-$55,000 are adequate, noting providers say they need around $70,000. Haskell acknowledges costs have risen since 2018 and providers struggle to deliver full services within contract constraints, saying DYCD is open to revisiting investment levels.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on adequacy of per-bed reimbursement rates

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In May 2025, the council raised concern that DYCD's extensions of RFY contracts without an increased per bed

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: reimbursement rate, which remained between $47,000 and $55,000 per bed, providers have reported that those rates did not reflect the actual cost of operating RHY programs or addressing existing program deficits.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Does DYCD believe that the current rates are adequate and cover the cost of providing RHY services?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And has DYCD conducted an analysis of actual cost of operating RHY shelter beds and compared them with current reimbursement rates?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: I think Commissioner has acknowledged that we need to do a review.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So I think we're certainly open to the idea that the level of investment needs to be reconsidered 100%.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And our colleagues, we are in touch with providers all the time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We understand there are concerns that costs have gone up since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And I think, you know, one of the things we hear from providers, like each one of the incredible providers that Commissioner spoke about, brings their own resources and flair and leverages activities.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And we have heard from providers that it's been harder to bring the full.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Breadth of services that they want to bring to to what to respond to what young people need and that they've had to remain largely focused on what their contract responsibilities are so we

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: we look forward to revisiting that so that we can make sure young people are getting all that they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know you guys are doing your own evaluations, but I've been talking to providers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They know what they need.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you guys just not gotten the feedback from them around the current debt reimbursement?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I feel like if they're saying we cannot provide this service adequately and then we're like, okay, we're doing evaluations, what does that meetup look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because that ultimately sounds like to me that young people then are not getting adequate services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so where are we at with the providers?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I feel like they gave me a thing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They gave me a price point already.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I think they said something about 70K.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We definitely have heard.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: What I would offer, yes, we believe providers, right?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Like we believe that the expenses that they have stated need to be looked at and considered.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And what I would say is that we have to evaluate our HY in tandem with our other portfolios.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And that's why this is taking a little longer than we'd like.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And we understand that that unevenness has created instability in the field.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So when we think about, and thank you for the acknowledgement about the compass, when we think about compass and we think about RHY and we think about beacons and we think about cornerstones, a provider is at the point of service.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: They are serving young people that are part of multiple programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And most of the providers are having multiple contracts.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So most of them are our beacon providers or our after school providers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So are our social services and doing our senior work and all the things.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so if there's an adequate one space, then it falls into other spaces too.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So the analysis is opening up the aperture and taking those things in tandem, not taking more time, but being really thoughtful so that any approach we have moves the needle evenly across the board.

chapters.summary: Stevens pushes on provider feedback about inadequate rates and the interconnected nature of DYCD contracts, noting providers hold multiple contracts and underfunding in one area affects others. Escamilla-Davies acknowledges the unevenness has created instability and says DYCD is evaluating all portfolios in tandem to move the needle evenly.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on provider feedback and holistic system investment

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: But it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And it's not easy to not feel like you're being compensated for the work that you're doing either.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, I mean, listen, it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And the problem is, and this is with the providers, I'm happy that you even said the story about a provider giving back the contracts because.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We're at a place where if we are not able to have adequate funded contracts, it is not okay for the kids because then they are...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're the ones who are not getting the services that they need.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, you know, thinking about providers, thinking about how do we push back and say, like, this isn't adequate and this actually now puts kids in danger.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to move on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I mean, obviously, I'll be back because, you know.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is what I do.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think that it's important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And when we're thinking about even all the other programs and how they're all interconnected and how are we looking at this whole system of investment for young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And honestly, I'm happy to hear that you guys are saying that you're trying to do an interagency conversation around like all the programs that young people have, because I'm a true believer that like.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's part of some of the problem where we have investments in certain areas where we'll get investments in ACS one year and the next year DYCD will get investments.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And like even when we're thinking about, I remember when I first came in, I was like screaming and yelling about getting 100 beds.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so it was like, oh, we got 100 beds.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But it's not funded correctly.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so it's like always this uphill battle.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And the reality is we should be looking at this holistically and looking at all the needs of kids and making sure that we're trying to hit all the buckets.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I just, especially with RHI, I just feel like we just don't talk about this enough because the city is embarrassed by it because it's sad to say that we have homeless children and they need support.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But it's not okay because even when I'm seeing the city roll out plans about housing, it's always an afterthought for our young people, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Why aren't we building housing?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: for young people coming out of the IHWA shelter?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Why are we not designating space for them?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so that's my goal for us to be thinking and looking at young people holistically and not just talking about child care and after school.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, what happens after that?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Those young people are important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I will continue to say it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If we're going to talk about a affordable city, we need to talk about it for everyone, including young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'll get off my high horse for now and talk to my next question.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: All right, so I'm going to move on.

chapters.summary: Stevens raises that after a 2017 Legal Aid settlement expired in 2023, minors turned away from RHY shelters increased by 3,000%. Tracy Thorne disputes the number, saying DYCD does not turn away minors and has a minor policy, with 316 youth turned away this quarter (down from 599 prior quarter), but those are not all minors.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on Legal Aid settlement and minors turned away from shelters

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In 2017, Legal Aid Society sued the city over access to shelter for runaway and homeless youth.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Under the resulting settlement, the city was required to prioritize 16- and 7-year-old...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: For placement in RHY shelters.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The settlement expired in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Since the settlement expired, the number of minors turned away from RHY shelters has increased dramatically.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Comparing the three reporting periods immediately before the settlement expired with the three reporting periods immediately after, the number of minors turned away from shelters increased by 3,000%.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How does DYCD explain the significant increase in minors being turned away from the shelters following the expiration of the settlement?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to my colleagues to dig into that number a little bit more closely, but we continue to, that policy to prioritize minors made good sense in terms of like the younger runaway and homeless youth are the more vulnerable,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: and we still want our providers to prioritize 16 and 17-year-olds over 18, 19, 20-year-olds if absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So that policy still stands.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We want to support our providers to adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the numbers in that report.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: You want to speak to that?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: The minor numbers?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: It would be a case of education and outreach.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I'm not sure where those numbers come from, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: But we do not turn away minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: We do service minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: As you know, our drop-in centers go from the age of 14 to 24.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So we have minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: In the drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: As far as our residential programs, according to OCFS regulations, we are allowed to have a minor under the age of 16 at a crisis shelter for 72 hours as we're looking for

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: placement and speaking to parents and speaking to ACS.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So I'm not quite sure where that number originated from.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We got it from one of our providers, and it was a report called Local Law 90.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I mean, 79.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So that will be the shelter access report.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And for our shelter access report, we have 111 youth.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, 316 youth were turned away this quarter.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The quarter before, it was 599 youth.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Which is a reduction of 280 youth not being turned away.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: That, you know, that's what we found in our report.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And as far as the age, those would not be considered minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Those are not minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Okay, so the 16, I'm sorry, I thought that you were talking about under 16-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So the 16 and 17-year-olds are the minors.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And there were minors on that report with the 316.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: But like I said, it's a reduction of 280.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The minors, we have a minor policy that we adhere to.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And minors are not just turned away.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: There is absolutely work done with those minors prior to them leaving our sites.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: We have really good relationships with ACS.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: We have a liaison that comes to our provider meetings and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Don't you worry.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I got questions on that, too.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Oh, you do?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I can wait.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Can we commit to following up on any minor who shows up on that shelter access report to make sure providers are clear about it?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: The priority.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We will follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And you guys know I get real iffy about language.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because even when we're saying it's a reduction by like 200, it was still 200 kids turned away.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I want us to make sure we emphasize that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I don't want us to be like, oh, it's better.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Still 290-something kids, which to me ultimately is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I just wanted to make sure I said that because everybody knows I get real crazy about language with the babies.
