chapters.title: Chair Stevens on unknown destination exits and discharge planning

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2025, 18% of youth exiting crisis services and 9% of exiting TEAL programs left with an unknown destination.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What efforts are being made to provide, what efforts are providers required to make to establish a safe discharge plan before a young person exits?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Everybody, don't answer at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Yeah, I think ideally every young person is adequately supported for their next transition.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think that we need to think about the developmental stages of young people when we're thinking about how...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Complete the information on where they go when they leave programs can be.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I know our providers are contracted to do follow-up services, and they may or may not have success following up on the young person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: There are instances where a young person may want to share exactly where they're going or the provider has trouble validating.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That number has gone down, I believe, over the years as we've worked more closely with providers in our meetings to say, like, it's very important that you make sure that you know where the next steps for this young person is.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: We're going to continue to see those numbers go down.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So there isn't a requirement for them to ensure that when a person is being discharged that they have a plan or some follow-up or something like that?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That is a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think the variable is that whether it's a voluntary program and whether young people want to participate in that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Listen, we all know young people don't like listening to us.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I get it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I raised a teenager.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They think they're grown.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I'm just trying to like, well, and if they don't.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, what's the step?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So it's just like, okay, well, I guess we don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is that what happens?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think many young people who are in the RHY system will continue to stay connected with a drop-in center, maybe not just one drop-in center, but many drop-in centers, and will very often come back to, or will sometimes come back to programming.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Something we see in the continuum of services with RHY is that young people are very often not connected with just one service, is that they sort of stay as part of the network.

chapters.summary: Stevens emphasizes the need for interagency data sharing to track vulnerable youth across systems. Haskell says Deputy Mayor Arteaga is prioritizing interagency data sharing and has begun conversations leveraging the new CIDI executive director's expertise.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on interagency data sharing for youth tracking

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think also, too, when we're talking about interagency stuff, that's why it's going to be important to make sure that we are, and I know there's like two rules of thumb.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Some people are like, I don't know, we don't want to track kids or things like that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I do think it's important for us to be able to follow up, to be like, okay, they were in this RHY shelter, and now they're showing up here and having some continuation, especially for these young people who are so vulnerable and can

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: fall victim to so many different things and thinking about, okay, so now they showed up at HRA.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, now we actually have a follow-up address that we could use because they're getting services from HRA or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I do think that it's important for us to figure out an interagency system where we can, as providers and as the city, be able to really support them and find them, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, I think it's the other thing sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know I used to be a provider.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, I'm going out there and looking for my kids.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know there's so many other people who would to ensure their safety.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Can I just say one thing?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: I know that Deputy Mayor Arteaga, this is a top priority for her, specifically.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: have interagency data sharing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And so she is in the process of leveraging the support and expertise of our new executive director of CIDI.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And so we have begun conversations about that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, because I mean, even thinking about like, I know,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There was, like, mention of, like, oh, like, if there's an issue, and sometimes they'll, like, reach out to ACS.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sometimes they're running from ACS because there's issues there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And now we've just activated this conversation with an agency who are going to put them back in a foster care system that could be abusing them or have issues with.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so it's like we need to, like, figure out a better strategy because it just doesn't work as easy as, like, when we're in hearings.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It makes it like, oh, we're streamlining this and they did this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I think that, like, those things are important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So it's like, okay, well, they were in ACS, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I think sometimes the providers are like, wait, they were there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, they must be here for a reason.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so it would further and have different type of conversations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So, again, I do think that there definitely needs to be some interagency stuff.

chapters.summary: Stevens notes a 31.7% increase in drop-in center usage in the first four months of FY2026. Thorne attributes the increase to expanded community outreach, a new 24-hour drop-in center in the Bronx, and peer navigators bringing youth into centers.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on 31.7% increase in drop-in center usage

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, so I'm going to move on to talk about some of the drop-in center stuff.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And including in the first four months of fiscal 2026, the city drop-in center saw a 31.7% increase from the same period fiscal year 2025.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What does this agency attribute this increase to?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I can take it.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Aside from the good work of the providers, there was much more community outreach

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: events that took place, as well as us opening up another 24-hour drop-in center in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And then FY25 is when they really got off and running with services.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: In addition, we also had peer navigators who were also doing community outreaches and bringing in youth into the drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And that's where the influx came from, intense outreach efforts and the work of the peer navigators and the good work of the providers.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether DYCD requires providers to make SCR reports solely because a minor seeks services at a drop-in center. Escamilla-Davies says providers are mandated reporters but DYCD is working with ACS to retrain staff on reducing unnecessary reports, noting some circumstances may require SCR calls to activate ACS services for minors needing guardianship.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on minors, SCR reports, and mandated reporting at drop-in centers

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What is DYCD regarding minors accessing RHY drop-in centers?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Advocates have reported that when minors seek service in drop-in centers, some providers contact SCR to make reports of suspicion, child abuse, or neglect.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Does DYCD require or advise its providers to seek an SCR report solely because a minor is seeking services in the drop-in center?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Under what circumstances are RHY providers expected to or required to make an SCR report when they're serving a minor?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I just want to start by saying that our providers actually absolutely would make an SCR report as mandated reporters for any abuse and neglect claims by a young person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: At the same time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're not saying that this is just for the abuse and neglect.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're saying anytime they have services, like are we requiring them when they come in for services that they call SCR?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think that, well, I wanted to share also that in our partnership with ACS, we've been working.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Alongside them to retrain providers and staff around mandated reporting and looking at disproportionality of reports and really isolating reports that are more necessary.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That's been an effort we've been training our staff so that they can work with providers and training providers directly.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So we want to minimize reports.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: As much as possible.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: There are some nuances when it comes to minors in a runaway and homeless services that in order to access ACS services where it's appropriate, they may need to start that with an SCR call to activate an investigation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What are some of those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, you know, I now have a recidivist CS, and I'm always yelling at them, too, around, like, people, young people, well, families and folks shouldn't have to get a report in order to access the services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what are the services that you feel like the providers would need to...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Put in a report to access those services.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: I think that's a really good question, and I'm going to turn it over to Sam to say more, and I'm sure our providers may have something to share about this as well.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: But the runaway and homeless youth services are voluntary services for young people who need a temporary respite or are working towards independent living.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: There is no custody.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: There is no guardianship.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And there are 16-year-olds who may be, you know, counseled by a provider where they really need more of a family support.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: They really need supervision and guardianship may be a better fit for them.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: That's a negotiation that we have with ACS.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: And to some degree, there may be some, and there are some minors, 16 and 17, who are better suited to the independent living and can do well with old young people and are ready to explore education, careers, health, mental health.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: So I think a lot of it depends on the individual circumstance.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: But if we do want to activate care.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Escamilla-Davies
utterances.text: Then that will have to start with an SER call.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: I do love what you're elevating here about what the impact of that call would be.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And so I really want to talk to kind of our providers more to understand not that it's done, but how it's done.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Because I do think that they lean into youth development principles and trauma-informed practices to make sure that there is awareness and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So I do want to come back to that question with the experts.

chapters.summary: Stevens presses on what guidance DYCD gives providers about mandated reporting obligations and policies for youth under 16, noting providers report confusion. Haskell says she wants to investigate further with ACS, and Thorne notes ACS attends quarterly provider meetings to discuss appropriate SCR call practices.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on mandated reporting guidance and under-16 policies

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Absolutely, because these questions are coming from providers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And one of the things they're also saying, like, because it's around what guidance you guys are giving them, because that's the next question.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What guidance are you?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Giving them around mandating reporting, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so obviously it's something that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I think that like sometimes with mandate reporting, right, I'm a mandate reporter.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I've taken that training multiple times.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But one, I think it has been evolving, especially around SCR reports.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It has been evolving because we know the disparities that it has and that we see in communities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But, you know, I...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: To me, this is a flag that it's clearly not clear across the board of what it looks like in each of the centers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's the next question around, like, what are you providing them as an obligation to mandate report?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But if you want to go back to the providers, I'm going to let you go back to the providers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I see a lot of them shaking their heads, too.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I think we trust that your questions are coming with an opportunity and an appetite for us to go back and see how we...

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: how we're making our recommendations, but also I think what you have offered here, and as Susan has spoken, is really to talk to the Commissioner of ACS, which I know that she's prioritizing training around mandate reporting and the levels and escalations.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So I'd like to look into this a little further.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, because even that, the following question is, while DYCD website providers give a list of specific protocols for 16, 17-year-olds, it does not include guidance for serving youth who are under 16.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And how do DYCD shelter policies differ based on the age of individuals seeking care?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And are those specific rationales on why policies were changed among minors?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I don't know if you guys had anything you wanted to add there, or we can move on if you want to speak to the provider.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I just want to add that Samantha had raised the fact that ACS comes to our provider meetings quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And the most recent meeting, we talked about the SCR calls and ACS's approach in reducing the SCR calls and what's appropriate and what's not.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And so we've been talking about that for a few years now, a couple years, too.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And we want to continue lifting it up.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And I just want to echo, yeah, I'm glad you're raising this.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And I think that this is a really important issue.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: But we are all working together to untangle the best way to work with 14- and 15-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So my providers, I'm sure they'll come back and tell me that you guys will have the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And then we'll keep talking because I do think it's something that we have to make sure that there is clarity and a basic understanding.

chapters.summary: Stevens raises provider reports that the streamlined DHS referral process takes 30 days, not the 20 days DYCD states. Thorne says policy allows 20 days for DHS placement but acknowledges it may sometimes take longer, with providers able to email her to escalate. Stevens notes the gap between policy and practice.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on streamlined referral timing, providers report 30-day delays

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And in real time, as per usual, my providers are texting me in real time around a follow-up question that they want me to bring up because...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're asking around the streamlined referral process.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so for young people who come in seeking shelter that day, how quickly can they bypass the intake process of the intake assessment that they have to be placed in?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because it sounds like, yeah, we have this bypass process, but it always isn't as seamless as it's being presented here today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So just how, like, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So how soon?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If they come in, they can bypass this process.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: I'm going to allow Tracy to.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Hi, I'll take the question.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So we have a process with DHS that offers DHS up to 20 days to place a young person from our programs to their programs.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: To find an appropriate fit.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So where do they go for those 20 days?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: They're in our shelter program.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So they'll stay with you guys for 20 days.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So they have up to 20 days to stay with you guys while DHS is looking for shelter.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So the streamlined process is for young people who are currently in our residential program.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So they're in our residential programs.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The providers look at all the different discharge opportunities for them.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And if DHS is the discharge decision, then that's the streamlined process.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And that could take up to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Real-time feedback.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They said it takes 30 days for them to hear back.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Usually when they hear back, it's a placement.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So it could take...

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Listen, if y'all turn around, the heads are shaking.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: They are shaking.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I probably know.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, my people back here are like, mm-mm, that's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So it might be what we have on paper, but that is clearly a place that we need to look.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Into because they're saying they're not hearing back for 30 days and you're saying it's 20 days for them for a placement.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So, and listen, I believe it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you ever been to DHS?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because if you think they get back in 20 days, that don't even sound believable.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And why would you believe that?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The DHS intake team has been really...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's overwhelmed.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Okay for us.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: They're doing a great job with this.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Yes, I will say.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That system is overwhelmed on so many capacities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And it's not for the lack of work that they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It is a system that is overwhelmed.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So we can't pretend like that's not true.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We all know that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so this is not a hit at them saying that they're not doing their job.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we know that they don't have a lot of staff because, well, I'm not in general welfare anymore.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I had been for four years.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They've been understaffed.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're under-resourced and all the things.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So that's why it's really hard for me to believe that in this instance that they have all their stuff together.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And I won't deny that maybe it does take 30 days sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: But that's what the policy says.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So immediate isn't in the policy, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I just want to say it's on paper.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: It's on paper.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But that's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're saying it's taking 30 days for them to hear it back.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what's the escalation?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: They can email me and I email the intake team and we help support them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're supposed to have 20 days to stay with the providers and it's 20 days.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But if they're not hearing back for 30 days, what's the process then?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I elevate the placement.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, I'm just saying, so do they get to stay in the youth shelter?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they can have an extension.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Listen, and it's not a shot at anybody.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think this is like the gaps that we need to talk about, which is why we have these hearings, so that we can have a moment to be like, wait, is this working?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, yes, on paper, it's obviously the policy, but...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's taking longer.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm sure it is.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Understand.

chapters.summary: Stens questions whether drop-in center clients can also bypass DHS intake, since drop-in centers are not shelters and don't allow sleeping. Thorne confirms the same streamlined process applies from drop-in centers, but Stevens points out the logical gap: youth waiting 30 days for placement cannot sleep at a drop-in center in the meantime.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on drop-in center bypass and DHS intake process gaps

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So if you go into a drop-in center, does that also consist of being able to be part of the bypass?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

chapters.summary: Stevens criticizes that only two street outreach teams with about eight total people cover all five boroughs, calling it ridiculous and demanding at least one team per borough. utterances.text: We've already provided 309 out of the 474 with other housing options.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so there's a crunch there that has to be done before the end of this year, and they're working really hard on that so that young people who landed in stable housing will be able to retain that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have some questions about the federal government stuff, too.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So don't you worry.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's coming up.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether drop-in centers will have access to the new HPD vouchers, since they are not residential programs. Thorne explains housing navigators at drop-in centers serve youth who are also in residential programs, and the details of voucher access are still being worked out with HPD.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on drop-in center access to new HPD vouchers

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I do want to ask a question still regarding the vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Will the drop-in centers have access to the vouchers?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because that's technically not shelter.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So trying to understand, will those providers have access to...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: These new HPD vouchers?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So we, you know, the commission mentioned how this is an ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So young people who are in residential programs are going to be going to the drop-in centers to work with the housing navigators around this new voucher that's being developed.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So, you know, the...

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The details haven't been worked out about exactly how, who and when and how and what it will be.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So we, I'm not, what was listed in the, in the,

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: But, yeah, what was the document that came out that said that there was the city hat project coming up?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Was it out of city council?

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: I was reading about it in the paper, basically.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: And so that's where, you know, we're still in the preliminary discussion around.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: How the vouchers will be accessed.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: The housing navigators are in the drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Susan highlighted the work of the housing navigators.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: We want that to continue.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So just if it's very specific about residential programs are the only place, it doesn't mean that the drop-in center folks will not be accessing it because young people...

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: At the drop-in centers are also in our residential programs.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: Young people access multiple drop-in centers to get all the services that they need often by their choice.

utterances.speaker: Tracy Thorne
utterances.text: So the line isn't as straight as...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, it isn't, which is why I think it's important for you guys to be a part of the conversation now.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You know, you guys are the experts, and I say this all the time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You're the experts in this work.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You're the one to, like, understand the workflow and understand diversity in the drop-in center or Shelton, how those things aren't the same.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And we don't want language to be developed that then doesn't allow young people to get access.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, again,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I think that this is a place where we have to make sure that you guys are part of the conversations earlier on and not later on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because sometimes I feel like folks just kind of forget, like, oh, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Hey, guys.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I don't want that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I want to make sure that we're working together, that you are the folks developing that piece of the policy and making sure that that's part of it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So that is some work for us to do and following with HPD.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about the impact of federal funding cuts on upstate RHY shelters and whether NYC has seen increased demand. Haskell says no influx has been observed, and as state coordinator she maintains close contact with upstate providers who know NYC services are available.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on federal funding restrictions and upstate shelter closures

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: All right, so we're going to move on to the federal funding restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Runaway and homeless youth shelters in other parts of New York State rely heavily on federal funding, including grants through federal basic center program.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Following the loss of federal funding, several RHY shelters in other parts of the state have been forced to close.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has ZYCD seen any additional strain on NYC's RHY shelter system as a result of RHY shelter closures elsewhere in the state, including an increase in youth coming to New York City to seek shelter or services?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We have not seen an increase.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: The New York State RHY providers are our partners, and we are in meetings together.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: They are fully aware of our...

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Programming and what we offer here.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: They have my contact number.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We're very close and we also share the same OCFS regulations and partners.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So they are aware of what we offer and if they need us, we will be there.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: But we haven't seen an influx of youth coming from upstate to downstate.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Do we track that?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Well, we track where the youth were the night before, right?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So there's a question that asks, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Or where your last known address, your home address.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So we would then know where that youth is exactly coming from.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Our partners in the state have made referrals.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: To our programs, but we haven't seen the influx of that.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about DYCD's communication with OCFS regarding potential federal funding reductions and contingency planning. Haskell confirms ongoing monthly meetings with state providers about the impact, noting the Basic Center Program funding has been around for decades but the city can only remain available to help.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens on OCFS communication and contingency planning for federal cuts

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you guys been in communication?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I know you said you've been talking with the providers, but have you been in communication with the Office of Children and Family Services regarding some of these closures that are potentially going to be taking place and how this is possibly going to impact

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: specifically New York City's RHY shelter system?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Yes, and it is.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: In addition to being the assistant commissioner for DYCD, I'm the coordinator for the state.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: So I am on all of the meetings with the other state providers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And we have been talking about the impact that it's going to have.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And like I said, they are fully aware of our services and know that we are here, you know, to help them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The next round of Federal Basic Center program funding is scheduled to begin October 1, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: RHY providers in other parts of the state raised concerns that additional funding reductions could lead to further shelter closures, potentially placing additional strain on New York City RHY shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is DYCD communicating with OCFS about the potential impact of federal funding reductions and RHY closures elsewhere in the state?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has DYCD accessed how additional shelter closures outside of New York will affect this demand within the city?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And does DYCD have a contingency plan if federal funding reductions lead to increased demand for New York City RHY providers?

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Yes, we've been in conversations.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: And like I said, we have monthly meetings where we are talking about the impact that it's going to have.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: You know, Basic Center is one of those federal funding that's been around for many, many years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: Back when I was a provider, we had Basic Center.

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: However...

utterances.speaker: Susan Haskell
utterances.text: We, like I said, the only thing that we can do on the city level is to be available and they know that we're here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, obviously we could be available, but also thinking about like talking to OCFS.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How are you guys also preparing for this?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know Kafka is now having their, they're going to be doing their coalition now and bringing that back.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I know we have some folks from the.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: From the state that's going to be testifying today to kind of talk about what this is looking like for them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I think this is another thing that we need to add of our long list of things to do around of like, how do we make sure that we are, or the providers are prepared

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: for if something, we do see a huge increase and then how do we make sure that we're able to meet that challenge?

chapters.summary: Stevens concludes the Q&A with administration, noting extensive follow-up is needed, then opens the floor for public testimony with instructions on decorum, two-minute time limits, and written testimony submission procedures.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens wraps up Q&A and opens public testimony

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think I'm done with the questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I am.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you guys for coming.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I really appreciate this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But again, just we have a lot of work to do in this specific sector and a lot of follow-ups.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So we'll definitely be in conversation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So at this time, I believe we are ready for testimony from the public.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you guys so much.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In-person testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I now open the floor for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Before we begin, I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As such, a member of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No video recordings or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But you may submit transcripts for such recordings to Sergeant of Arms for including in the hearing records.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you wish to speak today in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait for your name to be called.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Once you have been recognized, you will have two minutes to speak about the oversight topic of New York City Council's runaway.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, New York City Runaway and Homeless Youth Shelter System.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you have written testimony or additional testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You may email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Please note that audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When you hear a name, please come to the witness panel.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: For the first panel, we invite...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you do the names?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm over it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm sick of my voice.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I need to rest.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: For the first panel, we will be calling Nija Williams, Dylan Kelba, Samih Akanoishi, Reagan Robinson, and Sebastian Vontae.

chapters.summary: Sebastian Vontae of Safe Horizon describes operating two drop-in centers, a crisis shelter, and mobile street outreach. He highlights the impact of federal SNAP exemptions being removed for homeless youth, urges raising bed rates to $80,000, committing to release the next RFP, and including RHY youth in voucher program design and NYCHA N0 priority.
chapters.title: Sebastian Vontae (Safe Horizon) on bed rates, RFP, and youth housing access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: I'll go first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Stevens and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: My name is Sebastian Vontae, and I serve as the AVP of Street Work Programs at Safe Horizon, where we believe safety is a human right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We operate two drop-in centers, a crisis shelter, and mobile street outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Twelve years ago, when I interviewed for my first job at Street Work, one of the people sitting across the table from me was a young person in the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Today, that young person, today that person is a case manager on my staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: That is who I think about when we talk about bed rates and contracts, because every one of those things is what stood between him and the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: I want to tell you what he would be walking into today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: In February, federal law took away the SNAP exemption for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: people experiencing homelessness and for young people who age out of foster care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: So a 19-year-old sleeping in our shelter now has to document 80 hours of work a month or lose their food benefits after three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Many of them will not make it, and when the benefits stop, they don't disappear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: They come to our door hungry and we feed them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: That is why we are asking you to raise the rate to $80,000 per bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: The rate has not moved in years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Rent has moved, food has moved, security has moved, health insurance for staff has moved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Everything it takes to keep a young person safe overnight costs more than it did the last time anyone adjusted what we're paid to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We have absorbed that quietly year after year by stretching staff and trimming what we can afford to offer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: There is nothing left to trim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We are not asking for growth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We are asking to keep the kitchen stocked and the beds open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We are also asking DYCD to commit publicly to releasing the next RFP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Our contracts end in June 2027.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We cannot hire someone into a job I can't promise will still exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: And we are asking the city to stop treating our young people as a separate category,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: put providers and youth in the room when these vouchers are designed, give our young people access to homeless set-aside units and to NYCHA N0 priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: A young person in DYCD bed is just as homeless as anyone in a DHS shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: They just came through a different door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Regan Robinson of Covenant House NY urges reinstatement of $3 million citywide funding for the guaranteed income initiative, citing that 60% of Cash with Care participants secured housing and 70% gained employment in nine months. She also advocates for raising bed rates to $80,000 and including RHY youth in voucher rollout design.
chapters.title: Regan Robinson (Covenant House) on guaranteed income program restoration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: My name is Regan Robinson, and I'm the Senior Youth Engagement Coordinator at Covenant House New York, where I have the privilege of leading our Youth Ambassador Program, who you'll hear from three of them today, as well as our Guaranteed Income Program called Cash with Care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: I'm here today to urge the City Council to reinstate funding for the City's Guaranteed Income Initiative, which provided direct cash support to young people experiencing homelessness and expectant mothers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: In the first nine months of Cash with Care, more than 60% of our participating youth secured their own apartment or reunited with family, and 70% gained employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: These early outcomes show the potential of combining direct cash assistance with supportive services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: But the initiative operated for only one year, which is way too short to know whether these results can actually last.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: So ending the program now means losing the opportunity to understand all of its long-term impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: So we are here respectfully urging the council to restore the $3 million citywide investment in guaranteed income, including the $1.5 million for Covenant House New York's Cash with Care program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: This continued funding would allow us to build on what we've learned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: It would allow us to track our outcomes, determine whether guaranteed income alongside these supportive services can help young people achieve this long-term stability for housing and economic stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: We are also here joining.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: with other RHY providers asking for the increase in the bed rate for all existing DYCD contracts to $80,000 per bed, so providers have the resources to meet young people's needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: As the city expands its housing voucher programs, we're also asking that RHY youth have a meaningful role in the rollout through youth-informed program design, target outreach, and clear referral pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Dylan Kelba, a 20-year-old Covenant House resident, shares that he came to the shelter seeking safety from a dangerous situation. Now on a waiting list for his own apartment and selling art, he urges the city to increase bed rates to $80,000, include youth in voucher program design, and restore guaranteed income funding.
chapters.title: Dylan Kelba (Covenant House youth) on personal experience and policy asks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Dylan, I'm 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: I came to Covenant House because I was in a situation that was extremely dangerous and I needed some safety and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: What stood out to me immediately was how open and understanding Covenant House was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: The first question they asked me if I needed something to eat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: Currently, I am on the waiting list to get my own apartment, and I am an artist, and I've been selling art, and right now I've been thriving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: Today I'm asking the council to recognize the cost of providing support that organizations like Covenant House and other RHY providers offer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: I urge the city to increase the bed rate to currently, sorry, for current DYCD contracts to 80,000 per bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: So these organizations have the resources to provide quality care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: I also ask the city to ensure that young people experience homelessness are not left out of the rollout of the new city housing vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: You should have a voice in how these programs are designed, received outreach that speaks directly to their needs, and have clear referral pathways to connect them with available housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: I also urge the City Council to restore funding for guaranteed outcome programs that provide youth people experiencing homelessness with direct financial support as they work towards greater stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: Covenant House New York Cash with Care program shows promising results during the initial period, but continued investments is needed to determine whether these early outcomes can lead to meaningful long-term change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dylan Kelba
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Samih Akanoishi, a 23-year-old immigrant who lost his F1 scholarship at Stony Brook University due to illness, describes being turned away from adult shelters for lacking documentation before finding Covenant House, which provided a bed, food, immigration assistance, and CNA training. He now works at NYU Langone and lives in his own apartment through rapid rehousing.
chapters.title: Samih Akanoishi on immigrant youth homelessness experience

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: My name is Samihakhan Oishi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I'm 23 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I came to the United States as an immigrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I came to the States as an F1 student at Stony Brook University.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And as I got sick before the day of my finals, I found myself in the ER and so I lost my scholarship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: That's how I got kicked out of my dorm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And as I was...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Looking for shelters, I ended up in the Randall's Island where they could not accept me because I did have a stamp on my passport.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And the reason for someone to stay in Randall's Island was for them to be undocumented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: But because I had a passport, I could not get in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I was in...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I was there for about 18 days as I was looking for different shelters, and all the adult shelters asked for paperwork and documentations, which I did not have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Every time I would go to state ID, and they would ask me for my social security number, and I would get...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: There to ask me my state ID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: So it was going back and forth as a 19 year old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And as I was dragging my four suitcases, the door helped me to get to Covenant House.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And the only way they told me was to call every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: To every single shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And that brings me to a point where I was hearing everybody and the city has resources, but we need to connect the dots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And I know I'm going outside of my paper, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Currently, I am out of rapid rehousing program and living in my apartment,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: working in NYU Langone as a patient care technician while going to nursing school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I started my certified nurse's assistant program in Covenant House as I was living in the Bridge House in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: While living there, when I went there for the first time, two in the morning, all they asked me was how old I was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Not my paperwork, not my passport, not my documentations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And in a vulnerable situation like that, I did not care about anything else but to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: A place where I could stay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And as I walked in, they asked me whether I want to eat something, but I was too scared, as my parents said, don't eat something from a stranger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And I would not eat anything for the first 24 hours except chips, because those came in a package.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: As it may sound too good to be true, but Covenant House provided me with a bed, food, security, safety, and...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: They helped me with my immigration paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And I got my social security number and my state ID and work permit within a month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And after that, I got enrolled into the Certified Nurse Assistant Program and the health...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Care center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: They helped me with my health clearance because I did not have an address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I did not have a health insurance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I also got the help with my MetroCards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Simple things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: It's not something exaggerating, but also adult shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I have been into Franklin Shelter where I had to intake every 24 hours and I have to be online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: For that, but they could not accept me because of my documentation and lack of paperwork.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Where I'm standing here right now is Covenant House has shaped me in eight months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Where I'm standing right now, living in New York City, where I would walk the streets and feel, it's a huge city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Isn't there any apartment there I can stay?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And pay for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: And now after eight months, only after eight months, I can have that privilege to be in my own apartment while working the job and working towards the dream that I once had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: So it's not hard to have one less person in the streets because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I know the city has funds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: I know the city is trying, but it's important to connect the dots in between and have the right funds, which is they are asking $80,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Everyone is saying the same things, but I'm just trying to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samih Akanoishi
utterances.text: Figure out the whole experience where it's a whole circle where I don't have to go to somewhere else for and where I can be human not a paperwork

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much for sharing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Nija Williams, a 17-year-old Covenant House youth ambassador, shares she was kicked out by her mother and found support at Covenant House, which helped her return to school and graduate in the top 8% of her class. She advocates for raising bed rates to $80,000, including youth in voucher design, and restoring guaranteed income funding.
chapters.title: Nija Williams (Covenant House youth) on personal experience and graduating top 8%

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Nyjah and I'm 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I came to Covenant House due to constant issues at home with my mother and ultimately she ended up kicking me out of my home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: While I was at Covenant House, intake was pretty easy for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I was hysterical because I was so nervous that my mom was coming to get me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Because usually, like, kicking me out was usually, like, a punishment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: She would just have me standing by the elevator until she'd just be like, come on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: But this time, I left for real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: When I came to Covenant House,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: First thing they did ask me was, are you hungry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: You know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: They asked me how old I was and am I hungry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I said yes immediately because it was like 12 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: But, yeah, Covenant House kind of helped me get back into school because during my time and the thing that I experienced, school wasn't, like, my first priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: So I kind of started slacking, but Covenant House helped me get back into it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: And I just graduated from high school and top 8% of my graduating class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Regan Robinson
utterances.text: Congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You're not supposed to clap, but I'll let y'all clap because that's what we do in here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But don't go on nobody else's hearing because then you're going to get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we clap for the kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: And I'm currently a youth ambassador for Covenant House as well as the marketer for home care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Shelters like Covenant House give youth more than just a bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: They give us tools and support to reach our goals, whether it's school, career, mental health, or just finding stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: These are basic human needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: For young people experiencing homelessness, organizations like Covenant House can make the difference between simply surviving and having the opportunity to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: These programs provide much more than a bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: They provide...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: safety, stability, guidance, and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I'm asking the City Council to recognize the real cost of providing these services by raising the bed rate on current DYCD contracts to $80,000 per bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I also urge the City to make sure youth are included in the rollout of new city housing vouchers by including youth voices in program design, developing youth-specific outreach materials, and creating clear referral pathways for RHY youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: I'm also asking that the City Council should reinstate funding for guaranteed income programs that give young people experiencing homelessness the financial resources they need to move towards greater stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Covenant House New York Cash with Care program has already demonstrated a very promising outcomes in the short time it has operated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: But continued funding is essential to understand whether these early successes can translate into lasting change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nija Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens thanks the youth panel for their courage in sharing their stories, emphasizing the importance of humanizing the data discussed in hearings and encouraging them to continue civic engagement and advocacy, potentially even running for office themselves.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens responds to youth panel testimony

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is what advocacy looks like and continue to do this work because you guys are.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think that is so important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you guys for showing up.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.text: I have a couple of questions for this panel, though.

Vontae explains his organization runs the only DYCD-funded outreach contract with two teams of 2-4 people each, working 7pm-3am shifts covering multiple boroughs per day, and says having more staff and a team per borough would significantly improve coverage.

utterances.text: Sebastian, I just had a question.

utterances.text: I know Horizon, you guys do outreach.

utterances.text: Is that connected to your drop-in center, or is that part of the outreach team that does the borough-wide stuff?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: So we are the ones who have the two teams that go out into the boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.text: Two to four in each team?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: So there's, you know, there's.

utterances.text: And so what does the shift look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have so many questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sorry, guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: So an outreach shift is from 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: To about 3 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: And so first thing that we do when we get on, the first thing that the team does when they get on shift is review our phones to see if we've gotten any phone calls, follow up with any phone calls that we've gotten, and then dispatch to the area.

utterances.text: We'll bag up, like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We have like those RHY pamphlets that we give out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We also have pop-top food items as well as like, you know, quick snacks that folks can grab.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: We also provide...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
utterances.text: Needle exchange stuff, so Narcan and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So they're, like, fully equipped out there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, like, how do you break up with the boroughs?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, like, right, because it's like you have, you know, they're in Brooklyn, they're in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, how do you break it up, and what does the schedule look like?

utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sebastian Vontae
