chapters.summary: Maria Jarises of Housing Solutions of New York testifies that providing a bed is not enough; young people need trusted adults, mental health services, education and employment connections, and early housing planning to prevent cycling into the adult shelter system. She calls for better coordination across systems serving youth.
chapters.title: Maria Jarises (Housing Solutions of NY) on support beyond beds

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Stevens and members of the Committee on Children and Youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: My name is Maria Jarises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: I am the Program Manager for Youth Services at Housing Solutions of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak today about an issue that's very important to the young people and families we serve over our 31 sites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: At Housing Solutions of New York, we work with individuals and families experiencing homelessness and housing instability throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: In my role, I work directly with programs serving young people, and I see firsthand some of the challenges they face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: One thing I have learned through this work is that providing a young person with a safe place to sleep is extremely important but does not stop there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Young people also need support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: They need adults they can trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: They need access to mental health and behavioral health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: They need staying connected to school, finding employment, learning life skills, and preparing for their future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: And most importantly, they need a real pathway toward permanent and stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: When we evaluate our runaway and homeless youth shelter system, we should not only look at how many beds are available, we also need to look at what happens to young people after they enter the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Are they becoming more stable?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Are they connected to education or employment?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Are they receiving the mental health and supportive services they need?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Are we helping them move toward permanent housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: These, there are a few areas that I believe are especially important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Young people need access to safe and appropriate shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: No young person should be left without a safe place to go because there is not enough space or because the process is too difficult to navigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Second, the support has to go beyond a bed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Young people who experience homelessness may need help with education, employment, mental and behavioral health services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: benefits, financial literacy, and other services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: From my experience working in youth services, I know how important it is to build a relationship with young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Sometimes it takes time before a young person trusts you enough to tell you what they really need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: That relationship can be the beginning of connecting them to services and helping them make positive changes in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: We need to start talking about permanent housing early.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: We do not want young people moving from one temporary placement to another and then eventually entering the adult shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Housing planning should begin

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: As early as possible, and young people should have access to rental assistance, supportive housing, and other permanent housing options that meet their individual needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Lastly, we need better coordination between the different systems serving young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Youth homelessness does not involve just one issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: It involves housing, education, employment, health care, mental health, child welfare, and many other systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: We can expect a young person to figure out all this on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: As providers, agency, and community partners, we have worked together to make those connections easier for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: For me, the success of our youth shelter system should not only be measured by whether we are able to give a young person a bed for the night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: We should also ask whether we help that young person become safer, more stable, and better prepared for their shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: At Housing Solutions of New York, we are committed to continuing this work and partnering with the city, the council, and other organizations to make sure young people have access to support opportunities and stable housing they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maria Jarises
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak today.

chapters.summary: Edward Reyes of Inwood House at Children's Village testifies about the growing disconnect between DYCD requirements and available resources, arguing funding formulas based on bed utilization rather than actual service needs leave programs unable to meet complex demands. He calls for funding based on service scope, staffing reflecting youth acuity, and vacancy assumptions built into contracts.
chapters.title: Edward Reyes (Inwood House/Children's Village) on structural funding issues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: I'm the director for TIL program and crisis shelter for Inwood House at the Children's Village.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: I'm honored to be here today to speak about this growing issue and among my fellow colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: We've been working in collaboration with DYCD for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: And we specialize in just meeting youth where they're most at risk and emotionally vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: Despite the challenges, we ensure that these youth are safe, cared for, and guided toward independence and, of course, self-reliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: With this in mind, it's important that we address a critical issue facing New York City's runaway and homeless youth programs, which is a growing disconnect between what DYCD requires

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: RHOA programs to provide and the staffing and financial resources available to programs to adequately and successfully meet those expectations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: When these contracts and funding formulas focus primarily on bed utilization and minimum staffing requirements,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: rather than the actual needs of the young people being served, RHY programs are left attempting to meet increasingly complex demands with limited resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: This is not a failure of individual programs or frontline workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: It's a structural funding issue that requires city-level action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: So we feel strongly that there's a need for the following, which is to fund RHY programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: programs based on the actual scope of services that DYCD requires them to provide and not simply the number of shelter beds available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: These funding formulas should account for supervision, case management, crisis response, housing navigation, education, employment support, behavioral, health, and other required services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: We'd also like to establish staffing expectations that reflect youth acuity and service intensity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: A program serving youth with significant behavioral health issues, substance use, safety, and crisis response needs may require substantially more staffing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: than a program serving youth with lower levels of need, even when the number of beds is identical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: We'd like to fully fund adequate staffing across all shifts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: Many people don't realize that when you work in residential services, we're talking about a 24-hour facility that requires 24-hour supervision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: So additional resources are needed for evenings, overnight hours, weekends, holidays, and other periods when supervision and crisis response and supervision demands are particularly high.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: We also want to build vacancy and turnover assumptions into city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: Programs should not be forced to operate below safe and effective staffing levels because the positions are difficult to fill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: Employees are on leave or struggle with turnover issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: In closing, we just like to thank all city entities that are here and giving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Reyes
utterances.text: That's an opportunity to speak, and I thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Lade Swanson of the Ali Fournay Center reports over 400 youth on their wait list, 21-24 year olds waiting six months for crisis beds, and 40 youth nightly at drop-in centers preferring chairs over DHS shelters. They criticize the lack of communication about CityHAP vouchers, share that an attorney took money from their own salary to cover a client's legal fee, and announce plans for legislation to allow overnight sleep in drop-in centers by changing building codes.
chapters.title: Lade Swanson (Ali Fournay Center) on waitlists, voucher access, and building code barriers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: My name is Lade Swanson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Pronouns they, them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Director of Advocacy and Global Programs at the Ali Fournay Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: I know you share our outrage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have been doing this for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have done the convenings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have written the reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have come together as a coalition year after year after year saying the same thing again and again and again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And you are right that they're just embarrassed and our youth can't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Wait in crisis just because they're embarrassed by the mistake and we know what needs to be done and they should be jumping at the chance to fix this because it's not hard and it's not expensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have over 400 youth on a wait list at AFC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: 21 to 24 year olds are still waiting six months for a crisis bed and every night we have about 40 youth accessing our drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: They'd rather sit in a drop-in chair than go to DHS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We were so excited after, you know, 10 plus years of voucher that we got CHAPS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Very exciting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: It was really disappointing to hear that they knew almost nothing about it and haven't met about it, even though we're supposed to have these access to these in March.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: That doesn't feel so reasonable anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And so we need them to get together and we need our young people and our providers to be at that table because we can't fumble this after we finally got it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: I stand with my friends on ADK for...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We need case management and mental health providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We currently have wait lists for case management and mental health that we didn't have years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And the RFP needs to be released.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: I also want to direct you to the $15 million for LGBTQ immigrant legal services that we're trying to get in the October transparency resolution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We have 32% of the youth we serve are immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: We partner with Free to Be Youth Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: There's two attorneys for all of our young people plus seven other programs that they serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: One thing that I know will outrage you is the Urban Justice Center that does Free to Be Youth and the Sex Workers Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Last month had a client who needed $1,000 to pay for a legal fee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: They didn't have that money in the budget, so the attorney said, take it out of my salary so that they could pay for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: This is where we're at, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And, like, this should be embarrassing, and we are trying to do the best with what we can, but that should not be happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: I also want to name and let you know that I'm working on introducing legislation to fix the overnight sleep in the drop-in centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And we need DOB to change the building codes so that we can allow those exceptions into the beds, group B and A3 classifications for temporary cots and low barrier for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: And the second issue is how fast it takes, how long it takes to get these new sites online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: Are those 20 beds that you were asking?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: About earlier, our Casa Cecilia site, we've been ready for DOB to do a walkthrough since last summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: They just came in July.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: That's 70 youth that could have been accessing a bed in the last year, but it should not have taken this long for them to come through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lade Swanson
utterances.text: So we need maybe an exception for nonprofits that are doing this critical work for folks in crisis, domestic violence, R2Y, et cetera, to fast track these inspections so that we can get these beds faster.

chapters.summary: Mary Astrid Nussbaumer of Anthos Home testifies about helping over 230 young adults move from shelter into homes, recommending that all RHY have access to housing vouchers, funding housing navigation capacity, and funding one year of stability services. She reports 98% of households remained stably housed one year after move-in.
chapters.title: Mary Astrid Nussbaumer (Anthos Home) on housing vouchers and stability services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Chair Stevens, Deputy Speaker Williams, and members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: I'm Mary Astrid Nussbaumer, an aftercare specialist at Anthos Home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: We help New Yorkers move from shelter into homes faster and are a member of the Family Homelessness Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Runaway and homeless youth searching for permanent housing are most often looking for their first apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: They have no credit or rental history and no family to co-sign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Still, by providing necessary resources, the city can help them move into permanent homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Working with ACS and DYCD, Anthos Home has helped move over 230 young adults into homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Based on our experience, we recommend the following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: First, ensure that all RHY have access to a housing voucher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: We are grateful that youth and DYCD shelters are eligible for CityHAP, but the current funding will not reach them all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Young adults in our shelter system should not be denied resources due to the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: to their age or service provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Second, fund housing navigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: DYCD staff and providers like Aliforni Center and Covenant House already do this work very well, but more capacity is needed to find available units and make move-ins happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Third, fund one year of stability services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: By resolving arrears, providing financial education, and helping with voucher renewals, we can help prevent avoidable evictions and keep young people housed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: In our program, 98% of households were still stably housed one year after move-in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Voucher access and targeted support will help runaway and homeless youth find safe, stable homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Astrid Nussbaumer
utterances.text: Thank you again.

chapters.summary: Dr. Henry Love of Point Source Youth shares his personal story as a housing-instable queer youth who survived a suicide attempt, and notes 40% of homeless young adults report lifetime suicide attempts. He advocates for prevention programs like the Targeted Housing Assistance Program, which provides $3,700 on average within 48 hours and achieves 92% housing retention at six months, to reduce inflow into the shelter system.
chapters.title: Dr. Henry Love (Point Source Youth) on prevention and targeted housing assistance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Stevens and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: I'm Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Henry Love.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: I'm Director of Development and Growth at Point Source Youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And Chair Stevens, thank you so much for your leadership on this issue and your support for Point Source Youth in the past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: I'm a developmental trained psychologist with over 15 years focused on

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: fighting for and improving research programs, both design and implementation, for students and youth who are at risk of homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And just a bit about my story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: I was a housing-instable black queer kid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: In my early 20s, I tried to end my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: I'm alive because people caught me, not because the system did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: My best friend's name was Cordell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: He passed away at 24 because he was housing insecure and didn't get the supports that he needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: A few thousand dollars at a right moment would have been the arithmetic that changed his outcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Nearly 40% of young adults experiencing homelessness report a lifetime suicide attempt, and homeless high schoolers carry four times the odds of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And we've just heard from our provider colleagues and even an admin about the numbers of folks in terms of capacity issues with the beds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And let me be precise, because there was a lot of information coming out earlier from the admin about what's development appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And from age 18 to 24, the brain is still developing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Executive functioning, planning, impulse control, stress regulation, all of these things are happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And don't begin to finish until the mid-20s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: So that brain needs stability and agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And being turned away is an acute stressor administered by that system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And so shelter entry serves those routines, those relationships, that autonomy and development that is so critically important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And so we will not get out of this crisis on shelter beds alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And so that is why we're raising this issue today about prevention and also in that conversation in terms of getting to the important issue of getting to functional zero for youth homelessness, where shelter is rare, brief, non-recurring, and fewer young people enter it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Went through what the system can hold, and no one made more than 30 days to make sure that they get a place that they need to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: So prevention works and is cheap.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: The targeted housing assistance program on average gives out about $3,700.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And within 48 hours, we place people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And 92% have been...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Able to secure their housing after six months, 98% in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And we do have sites like you came to visit us at Henry Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: And so we are here today to, of course, advocate for those beds that are so critically needed, but to also raise this issue of prevention to make sure that we're driving down the inflow into the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dr. Henry Love
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Cornelius Wiggins of Mikos Light, formerly a homeless queer youth himself, presents findings from five community needs assessments of 650+ surveys showing 80% of respondents identified as trans/gender nonconforming, 67% hadn't felt safe in a while, and housing resources rated 3 out of 10. He calls for a comprehensive citywide needs assessment, stronger peer navigation, and accountability for outcomes beyond just providing beds.
chapters.title: Cornelius Wiggins (Mikos Light) on community needs assessment and LGBTQ+ youth

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: My name is Cornelius Wiggins, and I'm the founder of Mikos Light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And I spent more than 25 years working with homeless and runaway youth, particularly LGBT young people, young people of color, and young people navigating multiple systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: But before I ever worked in this field, I was one of those young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: I came to New York in 1999 as a homeless queer youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: I know what it feels like to enter systems when you are scared, when you don't know who to trust, and when the difference between one caring adult and one bad interaction can determine whether if you stay at a service or walk away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: These experiences why I dedicated so much of my life to this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Between 2021 and 2025, I helped conduct five community needs assessment with homeless and unstably housed youth all over New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Across the work, we collected more than 650 surveys, held 15 focus groups, and conducted 30 individual interviews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And young people told us very clearly what they were experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: In 2024, assessment of 214 young people, 80% identified as transgendered or nonconforming, gender nonconforming, 59% identified as black, 43% reported experience street homelessness,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: 67% said that they haven't felt safe in a while.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Young people talked about

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: harassment and programs, talked about misgendering, talked about unsanitary conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: They talked about retaliations after reporting problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: They talked about shelters roles that sometimes made it harder to maintain employment, education, appointments, relationships, and recovery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And when we asked young people to rate housing resources, the average rate was three out of 10.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: These numbers should make us ask bigger questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Are we measuring success by whether we give a young person a bed or whether that young person actually makes it into safe permanent housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Because a bed is important, but it is not an outcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And New York City currently funds a lot of programs, and those investments matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: But we should have to look at what happens inside those programs and what happens after shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Are programs adequately staffed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Are they receiving meaningful LGBTQ plus and trans and gender nonconforming competencies trainings?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: Not just one hour training once a year, but ongoing support and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: When a young person reports harassment or mistreatment, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: How long does a young person wait for housing navigators?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: How many young people leave shelters for permanent housing and how many of them simply disappear from the system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And do we even have enough data to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: That brings me to my big request.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: New York City needs a comprehensive...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: citywide community needs assessment of homeless and runaway youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: We need to ask young people directly what is working and what is not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: We should collect information about LGBTQ identities, gender, race, disabilities, immigration,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: and migration experience, parenting situations, involvement with foster care and justice systems where young people are arriving from barriers to housing experience and shelters and what happens to them after they leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: And young people with lived experience should be involved in designing the questions, collecting the information, and interpreting the results and the decisions that happens next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: We should continue to strengthen peer navigation and housing navigators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins
utterances.text: I watch young people respond differently when the person across from them understands something about what they've lived through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cornelius Wiggins

summary: The Committee on Children and Youth held an oversight hearing on NYC's Runaway and Homeless Youth (RHY) shelter system, with Chair Stevens questioning DYCD officials on RFP delays since 2018, inadequate per-bed reimbursement rates ($47K-$55K vs. $70K-$80K needed), capacity challenges with 319 youth turned away, and the transition of housing vouchers to HPD.

Youth with lived experience and provider organizations testified about the urgent need to raise bed rates to $80,000, release a new RFP, restore $3 million in guaranteed income funding, include RHY youth in housing voucher program design, and address gaps in street outreach, mandated reporting guidance, and building codes for drop-in centers.

Upstate NY providers warned that federal Basic Center Program funding cuts could close shelters and increase pressure on NYC's RHY system, with only 350 beds serving all of upstate New York and closures already underway.
